children: Down but not out — that would be the way to describe shares of Bloom Energy, which has emerged as a key bellwether for artificial-intelligence energy supply.

The stock rose 12% to $219.30 on Tuesday and was the best-performing component in the S&P 500 for the trading session. Shares made their way back closer to the 200-day moving average around the $221.40 price level.
It was quite the vote of confidence in Bloom Energy stock, which had fallen 43% as of the closing bell on Monday since hitting a record closing high of $345.85 on June 22.

Arguably even more impressive about the sharp share price increase Tuesday was that it came ahead of U.S. midterm election results in which American voters are expected to express their concerns around the data-center buildout.

Shares of the company, which supplies on-site power solutions to data centers, have been riding high this year, up 152% as of Tuesday's trading session. Investors have been confident that the data-center buildout will support strong demand for Bloom Energy's services.
That belief received a boost Tuesday.

"Demand appears to be inflecting more sharply than we previously expected," Barclays analyst Christine Cho said in a research note. She upgraded Bloom Energy to Overweight from Underweight but reduced her price target to $289 from $316.

"BE's accelerating capacity build, rising customer deposits and new supply commitments suggest demand is ramping faster than we previously expected, driving upside to our revenue outlook despite near-term free cash flow pressure," Cho added as way of explanation.

The firm believes that the sharp increase in customer deposits, increasing from a estimated $78 million in 2025 to $661 million in the third quarter, is potentially" one of the clearest indications yet" that Bloom Energy "is seeing a meaningful acceleration in customer commitments."

"We historically have not placed significant weight on customer deposits as an indicator of bookings, largely because it was unclear whether Bloom was consistently collecting meaningful upfront payments from customers. That appears to be changing," Cho said.

"As time-to-power has become increasingly important to customers, and Bloom has emerged as one of the faster solutions for bringing incremental power online, the negotiating leverage appears to have shifted increasingly toward BE," the analyst added.
The flip side to this strong signal is that stronger demand won't immediately translate to strong free cash flow or margins, according to Cho.
Not only is the upgrade a good sign for Bloom Energy, it's also an excellent indicator of continued demand for AI data centers and the AI buildout.
Wall Street has been grappling with concerns around the massive amount of spending needed for AI infrastructure and that has spooked investors.

The rate at which data centers are being built has also been called into question, with recent events in Texas and in Australia highlighting how residents have pushed back against data-center development.
Wall Street's worries about the AI trade recently spread from the so-called neocloud sector to the Big Tech companies that have been the engine for the AI buildout.
